clinicalPearls: The commonest of the idiopathic photodermatoses, seen most often in young women and typically appearing in the first strong sunshine of spring or on a holiday to a sunnier climate
The eruption is characteristically delayed, developing hours to a day or two after sun exposure rather than immediately
Lesions are itchy and 'polymorphic' (papules, papulovesicles, plaques or an eczema-like pattern), but any individual tends to reproduce the same morphology on each occasion
Intermittently exposed sites such as the V of the neck, the outer arms and the dorsa of the hands are affected, while the habitually exposed face is often spared
'Hardening' develops as the skin becomes progressively tolerant through the summer, so the eruption frequently settles despite continued sun exposure
Ultraviolet A is the usual provoking waveband, although ultraviolet B and occasionally visible light may be responsible, and ordinary window glass does not reliably protect

Management rests on photoprotection with clothing and a broad-spectrum high-factor sunscreen offering good ultraviolet A cover, with a prophylactic course of phototherapy in spring to induce hardening for troublesome cases
reference.pathophysiology: Polymorphic light eruption is thought to represent a delayed-type (T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity response to one or more endogenous cutaneous antigens that are generated or altered in the skin by ultraviolet radiation. Affected individuals appear relatively resistant to the ultraviolet-induced immunosuppression that would normally suppress such reactions in unaffected skin, permitting an inflammatory lymphocytic infiltrate to develop in sun-exposed areas. Repeated ultraviolet exposure gradually induces tolerance, or hardening, which accounts for the characteristic seasonal improvement, and a genetic predisposition with reduced regulatory immune activity is likely to contribute.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed history correlating onset with sun exposure, latency and seasonal pattern
Phototesting to characterise the provoking waveband and reproduce lesions where diagnosis is uncertain
Photopatch testing to exclude a photoallergic contact dermatitis
Antinuclear antibody and extractable nuclear antigen (anti-Ro/La) testing to exclude lupus
Plasma, urinary and faecal porphyrin screen to exclude a cutaneous porphyria
Skin biopsy in atypical cases to support the diagnosis and exclude mimics
redFlags: Facial or truncal rash with systemic features, arthralgia or positive autoantibodies suggesting lupus erythematosus
Marked burning or stinging within minutes of exposure, especially in childhood, pointing to erythropoietic protoporphyria
Skin fragility, blistering and scarring raising concern for a cutaneous porphyria
A new photosensitivity temporally linked to a recently started drug
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and tends to improve each summer as hardening develops, and it may lessen or resolve over years, although many patients continue to experience recurrent spring and holiday flares that are usually well controlled by photoprotection and, where needed, prophylactic phototherapy.
pitfalls: Attributing a persistent facial photosensitive eruption to polymorphic light eruption without excluding lupus erythematosus
Overlooking that ultraviolet A penetrates window glass and clouds, so exposure and flares can occur indoors or on overcast days
Assuming a high sun protection factor alone is adequate when ultraviolet A cover is the critical requirement
Failing to consider prophylactic desensitisation phototherapy in spring for patients with recurrent disabling episodes
references: British Photodermatology Group guidance on the idiopathic photodermatoses
management: Rigorous photoprotection with broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreen covering ultraviolet A, protective clothing and avoidance of intense sun exposure
Topical corticosteroids to settle established, itchy eruptions
Prophylactic springtime desensitisation phototherapy with narrowband ultraviolet B or psoralen-ultraviolet A to induce hardening before the sunny season
A short course of oral corticosteroids for severe flares or to cover an anticipated holiday in a sunny climate
Oral antihistamines for symptomatic relief of pruritus
Vitamin D supplementation to offset reduced cutaneous synthesis from sun avoidance
Exclude lupus erythematosus and cutaneous porphyria where the presentation is atypical before committing to long-term management
